recs.name: Dämmerung und Anbruch
recs.tag: He knew, one day, that he'd descend the mountain too.

lines.x: *sigh*...
Are you here to deliver meds to Mr. Czerny again?
Mhm.
Sounds rough.
Er, not that he's a bad person or anything, but it certainly would be easier if he remembered to show up for his regular treatments.
Yeah, I wish he'd be a little more mindful of his health.
But I guess that's what makes him who he is.
I'm gonna get back to work. Want to grab lunch later?
Sure.
Mr. Czerny, I'm coming in.
Come in.
Huh?
Based on past experience, she wouldn't normally get any sort of response, causing her to resort to more drastic measures – such as applying for a spare key card for his room.
But Czerny doesn't seem to be his usual reclusive self today, and the dorm's automatic door slides open almost immediately after his response.
What do you need?
Somewhat suspicious, she steps inside.
Strewn haphazardly across the room are leaves of sheet music, packets of various kinds of instant coffee, tomes related to Arts research, and a frowning Elafia standing in the middle of it all.
An all-too-common sight within Czerny's dorm room.
Most of the time, this scene signifies that he is deep in the creative process, and that nobody may interrupt him.
—In other words, many others from the Medical Department have already made such attempts.
However, the situation seems a little different today. There are no music scores splayed in front of him, nor does he seem to be composing anything.
If anything, this makes her somewhat angry.
Mr. Czerny, if you're not busy composing, I do hope you can remember to come to Medical for your check-up.
We've already made a special exception for you, so please don't take it for granted.
You came at just the right time, Hibiscus.
Of course I did. After all, you've been like this for more than just a day or two now.
If I wanted to start a piano class here at Rhodes Island, and take on some students, how would I go about doing that?
Huh? Well, uh, you should go to Logistics and fill out the requisite paperwork?
Wunderbar. Thank you, I'll head over there right now.
Huh? What??
Umm... What's this on the table...?
His last medical report?
Wait, Mr. Czerny! You haven't had your check-up yet!
...I had no idea so many people would show up after we announced he would be holding classes.
Excuse me, is this where I sign up for Mr. Czerny's piano class?
Yes. The end of the line is right over here. Please wait a moment.
Goodness, look how long the queue is! I told you to get up earlier, but you just wouldn't listen.
Mom, I don't wanna learn piano!
The instructor is very famous in Leithanien. If you miss this opportunity, there won't be a next time!
This is your one chance.
...Okay.
Ma'am, I've heard that Mr. Czerny can be difficult to get along with. Is there anything I should know ahead of time?
Uhh, I wouldn't worry too much about that.
Since coming to Rhodes Island, he's not nearly as hot-tempered as he was before.
Oh, good to hear.
Stand up straight, be attentive, and make sure you look ready to learn. Be on your best behavior in there.
I know...
Excuse me, is Mr. Czerny well-known even in Victoria?
Hm? Aren't you his assistant? And you don't even know that much?
Sorry, but I'm his doctor, not his assistant. I'm only here to keep things running smoothly, just in case.
Oh, a doctor? I suppose you don't know much about music then.
His Morgen und Abend has been making waves even through Victoria's aristocratic circles.
Makes sense.
Though, this is quite surprising. As far as I was aware, he only came to Rhodes Island for treatment. I thought I'd be lucky to hear even a single piece from him.
I'd always heard the maestro was rather eccentric, but I never imagined he'd be willing to start teaching. Would you happen to know why?
I... honestly don't know.
Maybe he wanted a change of pace.
Haha, fair enough. In any case, I'll be the envy of all the housewives once I get back from this trip.
What's wrong, Mr. Czerny?!
Sorry, something urgent came up.
Huh? Please wait a minute!
(*whispers*) That look on his face...
My apologies, sir. Please wait here. I'll go check on him.
Hibiscus's initial assumption is that he wasn't feeling well, so she follows closely behind him.
Unexpectedly though, Czerny does not return to his room, but instead makes a turn towards the training room.
Once he arrives inside, he plants his feet in front of a sandbag and starts pounding away at it viciously.
By the looks of things, he has a lot more vigor than she expected.
That noble, that damn noble, just wouldn't stop buzzing in my ears with his superficial grasp of music.
Does he have any idea how many misconceptions his children have been forced to accept because of his self-righteousness?
Music is nothing like that! How could it be?
His child's rejection of it is due solely to his own superficiality!
And the person before him! And the one before that!
Oh, that one wasn't so bad. They only wanted their child to have an appreciation for music...
Mr. Czerny.
Hibiscus? What are you doing here?
And here I was, thinking you weren't feeling well.
It's nothing much. Just venting a little frustration, as you can see.
Even back in Leithanien I used to encounter plenty of nobles like that.
They'd send their kids to me through Gertrude, hoping I'd be able to turn them into virtuosos.
Of course, I have no objections to teaching, but the majority of them didn't even really care if their children became pianists or not.
All they really wanted was a private performance from me, or an opportunity to strike up a conversation with Gertrude.
And even for those that truly wanted their children to become successful, it was only to the extent that musical skills would benefit their status as nobles.
On top of that, most of the children had already been indoctrinated into being dull or snobbish.
Or both even, a combination that makes my blood boil.
I'm glad you recommended I start exercising. It's proven to be a great outlet.
Czerny points at the sandbag.
Not everyone can be as pure as you.
I know that much.
In the Afterglow, I had neighbors who wanted me to teach piano to their kids too, just as a hobby.
Or rather, that was true for most people.
But at the very least, they were far more charming than the nobles, which is why I vastly preferred the atmosphere there.
I don't care if people lie to me, but they should at least be honest when it comes to music.
If you don't care for all the nobles who only show up for the prestige, then you probably shouldn't be holding classes.
Medical is also worried about your health–
Nein, that's not an option.
I need to hold these classes. It is a challenge I must overcome.
Well, if you really don't want to deal with the guardians, I can go talk to them myself and just ask them to send their kids in.
I can even forbid them from sitting in during the lessons.
That should make things a bit easier on your end.
Oh! That's a wonderful idea.
Let's go with that.
Mr. Czerny, it's time for your exam.
Mr. Czerny?
Dr. Hibiscus, are you looking for Mr. Czerny?
That I am.
I believe he's in class right now.
I thought this wasn't one of the time slots reserved for his lessons?
Oh, not his piano lessons. From what my kid's told me, he's been attending Hypatia's history lessons lately.
Huh. I'll go take a look.
Uh, hold on, Dr. Hibiscus.
What is it?
Since you're Mr. Czerny's attending physician, he's more likely to listen to you.
There are a few things I'd like to discuss.
Well, I can listen, but I can't make any promises.
Excellent. So this is the situation. My daughter told me she isn't able to keep up with the pace of his lessons.
As a matter of fact, this is a common sentiment I hear among the other parents.
We can understand his unwillingness to let us into the classroom, but you see, the pace of his class is—
Oh, far be it from me to suggest the maestro change how he does things, but perhaps he could consider a few small adjustments?
...Are you sure that's what the kids think?
Well, it's what my child believes, at least.
I'll bring it up with him.
Good, good. Thank you very much.
Now then, that concludes today's class. Incidentally, this is also my last day as substitute teacher.
Hypatia will be back starting tomorrow, so please look forward to it.
Thank you, Miss Istina!
Thank you, Miss Istina!
What's going on here, Istina?
That's what I'd like to know.
A few days ago, Mr. Czerny suddenly showed up for history class.
Hypatia thought he was just fooling around at first, but he actually took the course seriously and even took detailed notes.
The classroom is open to everyone, of course. Anyone can attend if they want.
Alright, thank you.
Mm... So that's how it is.
Whenever a student asks a question, they should be guided towards the answer, rather than corrected outright.
Their immediate understanding is far less important than building the bridge to arrive there.
Excellent. It was well worth attending this class.
Since when were you this studious?
Studious? Nein, I'm here to learn how to teach.
It has proven to be quite troublesome.
At first, I expected it to be similar to mentoring Ebenholz and Kreide – not particularly difficult.
That as long as they could keep up with my playing, as long as they could experience the wonder of performance for themselves, their level would naturally improve—
But I was wrong.
The fact is, most people cannot achieve even that much.
...I think that's perfectly normal.
I won't deny that.
But regardless, it has proven an obstacle for me.
When they ask me question after question, I don't know how to respond.
They ask things that, by all rights, should never have needed to be asked in the first place.
To me, the fact that they ask such questions means that their grasp of music is too superficial to even be considered beginners.
Uh, so you're here to learn how to teach?
Correct.
I now deeply understand how profound the educational process can be!
You... really are enthusiastic about this.
Naturally.
But why?
What do you mean, 'why?'
Oh, my apologies, Hibiscus.
I need to head to class. Can the check-up wait until afterwards?
...Sure.
Mr. Czerny's been running his piano classes for quite some time now.
Mhm.
A lot of our patients have been sending their kids, and some have even signed up themselves. A handful of our colleagues have been attending as well.
It took a while to set in, but he really is crazy influential.
Mhm.
What's the matter, Hibiscus? You're spacing out.
...I still can't figure out why he suddenly decided to hold these piano lessons.
I mean, when you've reached the very pinnacle of the craft the way he has, it's only natural to want to take on some students, isn't it?
Has he... really reached his peak?
You don't think so?
His music is already known far and wide.
I've heard that it's even been praised by Leithanien's Twin Empresses.
Moreover, I remember you mentioning that he personally fought the lingering echoes of the Witch King during the Afterglow incident.
And if he managed to survive even that, where else is there for him to go from there?
If I were in his shoes, I wouldn't mind starting a class myself – make some money, live a nice, cushy life.
I don't think he's that kind of person.
Then, what kind of person is he?
The kind who'll keep pushing the limits of music until his very last breath.
Do we not make exceptions for that sort of person precisely because of the respect we hold for them?
I suppose so. Otherwise, we would've strapped him to a table in Medical a long time ago.
But right now, someone like him is...
Come in.
Thank goodness you're here, Doctor.
What's wrong?
My daughter told me that Mr. Czerny didn't hold any classes today. Is he struggling with his health?
Please give me a minute. I'll go see what's going on.
Mr. Czerny. Mr. Czerny!
Pardon me, I'm coming in.
As soon as Hibiscus throws open the door, waves of sound wash over her. They must've been bouncing about within the room for a long time before she arrived.
Moreover, it isn't Czerny's music. Even an amateur like her can recognize that these sounds are very juvenile.
It must be his students' performance.
Their notes are interlaced with disorder, adding an extra layer of chaos to an already chaotic room.
Hibiscus has always complained about the messiness of the room, but right now, she is far more concerned about the man collapsed in the center.
Mr. Czerny?!
Mr. Czerny!!!
How did this happen?! All the indicators from your previous check-up were normal—
Huh? Urgh... What time is it?
Huh? Scheiße, I won't make it in time for my class!
Mr. Czerny?!
Oh, Hibiscus? Sorry, I must've overslept.
Did you come to make sure I'd head to class?
...No, I came to see if you were dead.
Oh. Don't you worry about that. I have no intention of dying until I've brought my students up to a satisfactory level.
What were you doing last night?
Ah. Do you hear the music? The students made it.
I wanted to identify the problem areas, then devise a lesson plan that would better suit their needs.
*yawns*... I suppose I've been a bit sleep-deprived as of late.
I have a question.
Hm?
The Czerny I know is a musician brimming with a passion for the arts.
But now, you're suddenly pouring all your energy into teaching.
To be honest, I'm a little afraid.
Of what?
Of the fact that you're acting like someone who's ready to give up on life.
Like someone who no longer cares about his own future, and simply wants to find a successor.
I'm a doctor, and I understand the pain and suffering that come with Oripathy. I'm not asking you to face it with a smile on your face.
However, you've come here to Rhodes Island. You should at least place your faith in us, and confront this challenge together!
Wait, hold on. You think I've given up on life? Me?
Huh?
Let me get this straight. You think I've lost my will to live, and am desperately trying to find a successor before facing my own death?
...Pretty much, yeah.
Is that really how I come across to you?
Sorry.
There is one thing I won't deny though.

When I was performing for the people of the Afterglow, sometimes I got the idea that someday I'd be standing on even grander stages, surrounded by even more people, and stirring their hearts with music.
But when I saw my medical report, it became clear to me that would never happen.
I don't curse my fate. Even if I weren't wracked with Oripathy, I would still inevitably die one day.
But even before that, I'd already experienced the greatest heights a musician could aspire to. I've been luckier than most.
However, obviously that was not enough for me.
I wanted to go further. I wanted to hear more. I wanted to keep composing.
Which is why I offered these lessons.
In other words, you didn't start this because you lost your will to live, but rather, you see it as a continuation?
That's not entirely true either.
It's rather difficult for me to explain it to you cogently.
Czerny is deep in thought for a while. He walks over to the window, and points to a mountain in the distance.
Let's put it this way.
Just as with many other endeavors in this land, music is a distant pinnacle that can never truly be reached.
My calling is simply to keep climbing that mountain until the end of my life.
But obviously, I cannot.
Even without Oripathy, there would inevitably come a day where I would be forced to descend.
But I do not see that as a tragedy. It's simply accepting fate.
These children who've received my instruction will traverse the paths I've walked. They will reach the places I've reached, and then they will aspire to even greater heights.
I hope to do this, just as many of my teachers did, and my teacher's teachers before them.
Through the process of teaching, they... No, I, do not think that my life is over. Rather, my life is continuing through music.
Because, while we are descending the mountain with a cane, these children will be happily embarking on their own journey to conquer music–
Just as we had done.
Just like the sun itself. At any given moment, it is both rising, and setting.
Oh, right. Before I forget, I've actually been working on something the last two days. I'd appreciate it if you could look it over.
What?
As Czerny says this, he pulls out a stack of papers from a messy pile of documents and hands them to Hibiscus.
Hibiscus's eyes are immediately drawn to the header – 'Request for Research Funding - Application Form.'
What's this...?
For a Leithanian, and myself especially, the synthesis of music and Arts is second nature.
But this might not be such an easy thing to understand for people from other countries.
I've analyzed this extensively, and feel that it has great potential. So, I've requested research funding for that very purpose.
So, how's that? That should address some of your concerns, no?
...I don't buy it.
Huh?
You might act like you're brimming with energy, but you haven't been taking care of your health. Just like back then.
If you really care so much about taking on good students, then you should take better care of your own body, for their sake.
...I must say, that's the most convincing bit of medical advice I've ever heard.
In any case, hand me those documents.
Now then, you should head to class.
Nein, nein, Hibiscus, that won't do. Can you go tell my students that today's class will be pushed back an hour?
What are you going to do?
I can't let my students see me like this.
I'll need some time to wash up and take care of my hands.
*sigh*... Sure, whatever you say.

recs.name: Before the Spilling Sunlight
recs.tag: He grits his teeth and tears open the fissure, light spilling out of it.

lines.x: 'Any energy left? Shall we walk another lap of the Afterglow?'
'Hahah. You finally admit I'm in better shape than you, then?'
'The sun's low now. The wind at night... it's cold.'
'I know.'
He feebly smiles. His pallid face shines gilded gold in the twilight.
'But I'm going to keep walking until the sun's down. I'm going to walk from first light to last.'
'Deep upon my mind, I'll sear this place that raised me, and imprisoned me, for twenty years...'
'While I can still spurn it, sing of it, despise it, and miss it.'
'Because I know neither I, nor my music, will make it out of our little Afterglow again.'
'Promise me. Don't end up like me. Do better than I did... okay?'
Welcome.
Your eyes are ruddy. Did you just pass by the Afterglow Hall?
My sympathies.
Much appreciated, Strollo—I mean, how rude of me, Gertrude.
That's alright. Not many are aware of this trivial preference of mine.
Even the retainers aren't used to addressing their Lehnsfrau by name. I've not been here long enough, simply put, and I and this city, this Spire, aren't too familiar yet.
Back to the topic, I just realize the inconvenience of this. With everyone busy today, you coming to the Cliffy Patio was the only option... Here, your medicine.
Danke.
The Spire guards didn't trouble you, I hope?
They intended to, until they read your note. Then they muttered something about it being 'outrageous' and stood aside.
There you have it. This Spire and I aren't just strangers, we're flat-out picking bones.
Not to mention, Czerny, as composer of Morgen und Abend, your name is known even beyond Vyseheim now. That's far more outrageous than an Infected or two entering the Cliffy Patio. Don't mind them.
(Sardonic laugh) Mind? It's not my first day as a commoner or an Infected... In any case, nobles like you are far too few. I must thank you again.
Don't rush to thank me, I didn't call you here just to collect your medicine. There was a favor I wanted to ask, too.
As long as it's within my power, then by all means.
I'm hoping you can perform Morgen und Abend for my brother's funeral.
I know it's somewhat of an ask. You'd have to arrange the flute and cello into solo piano, but even then...
No, I understand. You're utter strangers in a sense. Lehnsherr and subject, whatever that counts for.
But he... let me find the words. He didn't rule like my iron-fisted father before him. He was a vacillatory kind of man.
To put it unkindly, he was weak.
But because he was so irredeemably weak compared to Father, he was much less harmful. Not just to me, but to his own subjects—
Gertrude.
Yes?
No need to describe him so painstakingly. I know the feeling of losing a loved one.
I paid a visit to my mentor just before this. In your manner, she has little good to say about her daughter. She calls her stubborn, disobedient, unappreciative...
But once she has no more to say, she weeps too hard to breathe.
It is what it is to be vulnerable. Masking it by lambasting the dead hides nothing.
I know the Graf's funeral will draw great attendance from nobles, and you're quite used to striking two fowls with one stone, so my guess is...
Correct. Your patron will be inviting many music critics.
You have quite a reputation already, but it's still not enough... Yes, let's be frank. It's far from enough. We must grab every opportunity we can to boost your fame.
Even your elder brother's funeral?
If it were a private remembrance, I would be glad to perform Morgen und Abend. However, before such stuck-up nobles and holier-than-thou critics...
It's you who needs the consolation at this time, Gertrude. Not them.
I know it doesn't take your fancy. When it comes to music, you're forever pure. I, though, am not you.
Those things you find insignificant—money, fame, connections... I have to care. The artist can focus on one thing only, but the patron cannot.
Gertrude...
Think about it. Okay?
Suppertime, Mein Herr!
Mein Herr—
Ursula, thank you, I heard you. Please lower your voice.
...Have you been waiting for me this whole time?
That I have.
Tell me, what's the matter now? You were finally in good spirits for once...
Gertrude had a... request for me. She's asking I perform Morgen und Abend at her brother's funeral.
And how can you say no, when she's your very own patron?
...They are laying a noble to rest in a public service, Ursula.
Performing Morgen und Abend, for me, is like... tearing off my own shell... displaying the most vulnerable part of me to someone else, hoping they'll understand, that they'll resonate with it.
Tell me to perform it for you, for Gertrude, for anyone in the Afterglow you like, and it would be my delight. Because I know you would understand me.
But those nobles, those critics... what will they understand? The technical prowess? Maybe they'll echo that one certain baffling review of the piece...
'The composer's meager stature is so far short of the musical ambition as to unbalance the whole thing'?
Why should I have to make my vulnerability into a show for them? For the fame? The money?
Oh now now, slowly, Mein Herr, slow down. First we have some supper, yes?
Reports of the remnants' movements, gathering points of private arms... *sigh* Oh, dear brother, you.
Dame Strollo—
What is going on? You—aren't those papers confidential?
All the more reason to feed them to the fireplace.
And by the way, Lachmann... it's been quite a few years since 'Herr Caster' planted you in Vyseheim.
Don't worry, 'he' was my father's handler, then my brother's, and now mine. I don't plan to change anything there.
...I thank your graciousness, Dame S—Dame Gertrude, excuse me.
We need the funeral sorted before we make our next move. What's still unaccounted for?
I believe you know exactly what.
Those critics are gushing with the honor of being invited to a Graf's funeral, but should the musician himself fail to show...
Hah, yes.
He's a fool. Such a fool he'd turn away a silver platter of fame and fortune.
And that very foolishness is key. Morgen und Abend could only have been written in his longing for Fanny, not in mine for my dearest brother.
If you truly want this sentimental man fiddling in the palm of your hand, perhaps you should take things to the next level with him personally...
Not one more inappropriate suggestion. He has no such interest in me. Getting him to see me as his generous patron, the most trustworthy of his friends, is enough.
But if...
You think all my efforts will be for naught on the off-chance he doesn't turn up, correct?
He will.
You have a backup plan?
'Backup plan'. No, I simply know him well enough.
Or perhaps I should say, he's too blindingly simple of a person. One casual chat and you've already hit his deepest depths.
What do you mean by 'that was when you started waiting for me to eat'? Always I waited for you before supper, you hear.

I remember one time Fanny came to tell me there was an error in one of my counterpoint exercises, and I pushed away my plate and rushed right to my mentor's home to quarrel with her until the dead of night...
I came home on an empty stomach to find the table cleared, nothing left.
How was I supposed to know they'd have no food that day, eh. Besides, didn't I bring over m'own catering for her the next day?
...On which Fanny burnt her tongue.
And you almost dropped m'roast potatoes on the floor.
The potato soup's still warm, now, have another bowl.
Hrm.
Who's there? Let yourself in, it's open.
Come on in, come on in!
So much easier to find your place now, Frau Ursula.
The Herr fought for that, y'see.
Hahah, he's fought for much more than himself!
Congrats to you all on the new home, and congrats to you, Czerny, it feels like yesterday you were a little brat and now you've done something we could never dream of and become talk of the town!
*clicks tongue* What a splendiferous place... What's this, a bathtub?
I haven't seen one of these in years, now. Frau, how's it to use?
You're asking? M'bone joints used to itch each time it rained, oh, terrible, I couldn't stand it. Now with all the Herr's done, I dip in the tub and m'body comes out sixty years younger!
You see that, Czerny, Frau Ursula's life is never better! That's you, you made it happen!
Mrm... mm.
Here, take this! Fine wine, the finest, they love it all day in the Cliffy Patio. If you knew how long it took me to get it from that asshole running the cafe...
You're too kind, too kind. We're havin' supper right now, stay and have some, ja?
No need.
There was this whole party of people the other day, couldn't tell you where from, come 'in search of the place where the great composer Czerny was born'.
At that very same time I was drumming up customers with my accordion, and whoof, good day for the ol' fried sauerkraut stand. If I ever get business like that again, oh, you bet I'm there.
Right, you get on with it!
Mein Herr, what's the matter with you? Someone drops by, and he's here to housewarm you. You don't even say hello?
I was quite a hassle to him before, so it's just... a little awkward for me.
Hassle? Oh, that fight, you mean, the one you had.
*clears throat*.
Old news, old. You told him sorry, and you heard him, you were just caring too much, that's all. Him, he holds nothing against you.
That was...
I know, you're not too good with words. The whole Afterglow knows, ja? We know.
But I'll tell you what you do have, now. It's too much temper.

Fräulein Fanny, when she couldn't taste the food she ate? She didn't know up from down she was so sick, that's why she thought, gosh, they must be doing it to me on purpose. Then you come along and get carried away with it, why?
Scared the daylights out of me when you stormed up to his stand, never saw you so furious in all my life—
...My bad, my bad. Eat, go on, let's eat.
Ursula.
What is it, Mein Herr?
Would you say, if I went to that funeral, then more of that... business, that the Herr mentioned, would come in?
If I should show my weakness to the ones who don't give a shit about our fates, to let them scrutinize me, then would the Afterglow... have a few more houses with bathtubs, maybe?
Mein Herr...
No, this is wrong. This isn't how music should be. At least not my music.
But...
'Because I know neither I, nor my music, will make it out of our little Afterglow again.'
'Promise me. Don't end up like me. Do better than I did... okay?'
Mein Herr, where're you off to?
Gertrude.
The sooner I accept her invitation, the sooner I can start arranging Morgen und Abend for solo piano.
Time flies.
The previous Graf Strollo's funeral is already halfway through. The performance is set to begin.

Czerny lifts his head, looking into the distance. The lofty buildings of the Cliffy Patio enter his vision, yet in his mind's eye, he sees that afternoon with Fanny, passing by the Afterglow Hall again and again.
He gives an imperceptible bow to the crowd, seats himself, and begins to perform.
They had an Infected play for this funeral?
Obviously she's seizing on her brother's death for the chance to sell more records.
A piano solo? I highly doubt whether a single piano grants him enough to evoke both a flute and a cello's manners at once.
The musician's ears are sharp. He hears every ill-willed voice picking away at him, before the performance is even truly underway.
He bites at his tongue in regret, but it's too late to stop playing now.
He's already heard everything, but he needs to force himself not to hear anything.
The melody trickles through the grounds. The noise doesn't subside, and yet, it gradually begins to fade away from him.
Morgen und Abend.
From first light to last.
If a flute is clarity, light, expanse, like an unbounded sunrise atop the hill, then the piano's morning sun is addled by a shawl of mist.
Sunlight bathes the earth in equal measure, never dwindling for the parched, nor strengthening for the clouded.
The wisps of chill emanating from the first light feel almost ruthless.
...Bold arrangement.
I still don't think it's quite on the mark. Can you really call this morning sun? What could a morning sun like this possibly illuminate?
Perhaps nothing at all.
He's quite engrossed.
I'd posit it's the first he's ever performed for so much nobility. He'd do well to seize the chance.
But if you ask me, Strollo—and not the one flitting around the attendance, I mean the one in the coffin—he's had the short end of the stick.
The man spent so long living in his father's shadow, and he could barely come into power himself before illness whisked him right back out. To boot, an Infected playing at his funeral.
From first light to last.
A hammer can never shudder the listener's heartstrings as the bow does, stirring the doleful scarlet shadows of the setting sun.
And so, he chooses to perform the most ordinary afterglow one could know.
The sun is setting soon. It's time for us to go to sleep.
Hurried gasps. The scent of bed. That orange ceiling. The scattered stars glimpsed through deep blue curtains.
At its jet-black nadir, the night holds the departed close. The light still lingers. The musician, ignoring them all, performs that deep, shivering green where light and dark intertwine.
Violent yet tranquil, profound yet mundane. The most ordinary of forever partings.
Graf Strollo, you tragedy... *sigh*.
Timid, shrunken bastard. Laughed at his own words as if apologizing for everything he said, even after succeeding the title.
The last time I saw him, he gave me the wrong gift. I jeered at him to my heart's content... And now, damn it all, it's like he's still there, laughing along.
What drives me to do that, my god—
...Shh.
(Sniffs)
From first light to last.
The sun climbs up in its track, up to its apex, so high as to steal the breath from you. Then in gentle leisure it descends, until the murk of twilight, until it sinks into the earth.
In the face of the sun, we are insignificant, exposed, our wealth of emotion our greatest treasure, one amounting to so, so little.
If we could tarry just a little longer in this mortal coil, could we see the pain vanished, the wrinkles smoothed, the love we've lost made young by the dusk of rising east and dawn of setting west?
But we are no more than motes in the confines of time. In the end, we part.
A thorough and achingly open parting.
The final note disappears into the late rays' winds.
They blow it away from Vyseheim, to some place far beyond the eye, and only then do the whispers finally surface again.
Now these murmurings are solemn and restrained, interspersed with low sobs.
...You know who I'm reminded of? My uncle. A veteran who retired from the field, terrible temper. Never much humored me. And then eventually he became senile.
I visited him once before he passed. Just so happened to find him burning his things in the garden. The wind came and carried away all that paper ash, like grey snow falling into the sky.
Czerny, Czerny...
My god, there's nothing fair about a man's fate. How could he have been born here? How could he be an Infected?
You're quiet.
(Sniffs) I... *sigh*... what else can I say? What am I fit to say?
Once I'm home, once I've calmed down, I'll write a mild review. You know, that's highest praise coming from me. But for now—
(Takes a deep breath)
Let's talk about something else. Have you noticed Herr Ed? He's the most esteemed of the critics Dame Strollo invited here, but I haven't seen him at all.
Dame Strollo was just looking for him at the burial site.
Just? While Herr Czerny was playing?
Yes.
Czerny slowly lets out a very pent-up breath.
His ears are sharp. He's heard everything, the voices flummoxed by prejudice, yet shaken by art... by their own vulnerability.
He wipes the tears from his face, and incidentally catches sight of Gertrude.
Herr Ed, I count my blessings that you suffered no misfortune while lost in the Afterglow alleys.
The onus lies with me, that I had you so graciously lead me out, and miss Herr Czerny's performance in the process.
I wouldn't be so sure. Didn't we hear it, even from where we were? What beautiful music.
Gertrude forgets to hide her formality smile as she turns her head, forgets to switch to one of grief, and that is how she makes eye contact with Czerny.
Once she takes notice of how incongruous the musician's red eyes and her own expression are, only then does she realize she's made a huge mistake.
Would that she could take it back, she thinks, as she maintains the smile on her face, leaves the critic it was meant for behind, and quickly paces over to him.
As she expected, Czerny is also walking up to meet her.
What is Czerny doing? Striding right over to Dame Strollo? Not one acknowledgement for the audience?
...As is fair. They must have a lot to talk over.
This... is how you mourn your brother?
...The artist can focus on one thing only, but the patron cannot.
The setting sun hangs west. Both take pains not to look at the other's face again.
Don't.
...Fine. It's your turn to grieve for him.
Czerny hurriedly leaves the Afterglow plaza. No greeting. No stopping. No one enters his eyes.
Mein Herr, letter for you.
From who?
...Gräfin Strollo.
You haven't talked for a month. What if...
An invitation card... and a penned letter?
You want to invite me a second time, Gertrude... Dame Strollo?
No, first, let's see what she wrote.
Find you well, how do you do... this is hollow rubbish.
Wait, what is this in her postscript...

lines.st: 'I won't apologize for the funeral, nor for never grieving over my brother. I apologize that I cheated you.'
'If you'd believe it, I came to realize afterwards I only accomplished one thing.'
'I had an Infected perform a piece at Graf Strollo's funeral, sending my dearest Strollo family... 'best wishes'. Ridiculous, isn't it?'
'...I'm astonished I just tacked on such carelessly offensive words.'
'It seems, in the end, we're not the same.'

lines.x: Gertrude, you absolute...
This... isn't even her invitation. Is this... a tour?
A tour?
Critics and nobles all wanted me to perform in their cities after that funeral, so she went and drew up a 'tour'...
'The artist can focus on one thing only, but the patron cannot,' you say?
...*sigh*.
Ursula, what do you think about the tour?
An Infected on tour... I can't imagine how it might turn out, but I'm sure it wouldn't be like on holidays.
What an understatement. I'd practically be an exotic sideshow animal...
But I must go.
What for?
I simply believe the sound of my strings, an Infected's strings... is enough to cross the widest gap, and plunge into those nobles' hearts.
Even if I'm uncompensated, even if I'll be some rare creature to gawk at, just put a piano in my cage...
Even if all I have is a metal stick to strike at my bars, I'll be more than willing.
Just as Czerny expected, the tour of an Infected musician is akin to an exotics display.
Even now, on the very last stop...
The streets have been emptied to allow this Infected to walk to the venue on his own. None are willing to walk with the Infected, save for an impatient bodyguard.
Out of nowhere, in the faintest strains, he hears the most familiar music. It comes from a roadside garden.
Morgen und Abend?!
Don't stop! Move!
Mein Herr, whose garden is...
The Markgraf's family cemetery! Move it, move!
Czerny begins his stride, as he lifts his head to the sky.
The city's overcast almost resembles the night sky. The irregular schedule of the tour has messed up his body clock. He just wants to sleep.
He barely has any energy left.
But still he'll keep this ailing body going, to make another lap of this dwarfing mortal coil they call life, around and around, onward and onward.
He'll spurn, sing, despise, miss...
From first light, to last.
